persona: The first look: has never played FFX or FFX-2; sees one frame as a store screenshot or trailer still on a phone or laptop and decides in two seconds whether it looks premium enough to wishlist. Clutter, confusion and amateur seams lose; a striking, clear image wins.

F01.note: The dragon fills the phone screen and the buttons are big and obvious, but the bottom fifth is dead black and one button slot sits empty, so it feels unfinished.

F02.note: Low behind Tidus, the party bunches into one knot in the middle, Kimahri all but disappears behind him and the top half is empty sky.

F03.note: The gilded theatre frame is a bold idea, but the menu, turn list and health bars collide with the curtains, so it reads cluttered and gimmicky.

F04.note: The villain looms big on the left right up against the menu while the heroes are specks far right with a name tag sitting on Kimahri; I cannot tell where to look or which side is mine.

F05.note: Persona-style three-panel split is loud and exciting, but the menu sits on Tidus's portrait and the health bars on the villain's face.

F06.note: Cinematic letterbox and lovely bokeh, but the hooded white mage's back hogs the left and the dragon is small behind Paine.

F07.note: Clean classic diagonal in a detailed lamp-lit corridor; every girl and the dragon are clear, solid rather than jaw-dropping.

F08.note: The dragon alone against blur with big portrait cards reads instantly, but with no heroes on the field it feels like a menu screen and the dragon floats.

F09.note: Film-style bands keep the painting clean and the faces visible, but Kimahri hides behind Tidus and the top band is fussy with tiny labels.

F10.note: The villain towering over the heroes' backs is dramatic, but the party is squeezed between the menu and the health panel.

F11.note: Mirrored diagonal with the villain up-left and a moon over the party is attractive, but HUD blocks on both sides make it feel busier.

F12.note: Huge dragon over a tiny party huddle: great scale, but the three girls overlap into one cut-out clump.

F13.note: Round portrait tokens on a blue map look like a debug board, not a game.

F14.note: The rim-lit villain seen from behind is moody, but at a glance the big figure looks like my character and the heroes are small in the distance.

F15.note: Close behind the girls with the dragon looming is punchy, but the white mage is cropped and the dragon's tail runs under the health panel.

F16.note: Bright blue, soft bokeh and the whole party in a clean diagonal toward the villain: polished, though the menu clips Tidus's sword.

F17.note: Pulled back behind the party, the dragon shrinks to a small shape over a huddle, with lots of empty blur.

F18.note: Good over-the-shoulder menace, but the heroes huddle and the picture feels crowded between the HUD blocks.

F19.note: The clean corridor diagonal with the background melted into orange bokeh: moody and cinematic, a little less sense of place.

F20.note: Tidus's back centred with Kimahri and Yuna fanned out and the villain beyond: the most heroic of the full-screen over-the-shoulder shots.

F21.note: The dragon rears above the three girls' backs with room to breathe and the HUD out of the way: dramatic and clean.

F22.note: Almost the same as the dragon-over-backs shot but tighter; the wing meets the menu and the tail runs under the health panel.

F23.note: On a phone this is a poster: villain looming, heroes' backs, big clear buttons and health cards; instantly premium.

F24.note: Stunning key-art pose, but it is a poster, not a battle: no menu, no health, and the girls have their backs to the dragon.

F25.note: A giant close-up face beside the dragon with the boss bar pasted across her hair looks like a collage.

F26.note: The neon-outlined dragon silhouette is striking, but the menu covers it and the party are tiny in a dark void.

F27.note: The three-panel split with the white mage portrait and dragon close-up is vivid, but the menu and health bars pile onto the dragon panel.

F28.note: Letterboxed over-the-shoulder with snow falling: heroes facing a looming villain and every number tucked into the bands; cinematic.

F29.note: Gorgeous key-art composition under the moon, but there is no HUD and the heroes stand with their backs to the villain: a poster, not a fight.

F30.note: Crisp painted crags and a moon behind a clean diagonal; attractive and readable, a touch busier than the soft-focus version.

F31.note: The villain alone, big and sharp over portrait cards, is bold and clear, but with no heroes on the field it feels like a menu.

F32.note: Beautifully detailed machinery backdrop, but the party is a small row and the lower half is empty floor.

F33.note: Too tight: Tidus's and Yuna's backs, the claw creature and the villain pile up and Kimahri vanishes.

F34.note: Tidus's giant face grabs the eye, but the menu lies across his chest and a pixelated seam where he meets the villain looks broken.

F35.note: Mirrored over-the-shoulder works, but the dragon crowds the boss bar and a hint tag lands on its belly.

F36.note: Mirrored wide side view with a nice detailed wall, but everyone is small and the menu crowds Paine.

F37.note: The high tilt-shift view makes the heroes tiny and blurs the villain, the one thing I want sharp.

F38.note: The white mage turns toward me with the dragon waiting on the right, framed by clean bands: the best character shot of the dragon fight.

F39.note: Theatre frame again: a charming stage spotlight, but the HUD fights the gilded frame and the curtains.

F40.note: Dramatic long shadows from above, but the party is scattered on both sides of the dragon, so I cannot tell which side is mine.

F41.note: Real depth from the soft foreground white mage to Paine at the dragon's feet; it feels three-dimensional, though the dragon is a touch small.

F42.note: Wide establishing shot with pretty mountains, but everyone is small and half the screen is empty floor.

F43.note: The villain is colossal, great scale, but the heroes look pasted onto his robe.

F44.note: An overhead tactics grid reads as a different genre: dark, with a small dragon and a tiny party.

F45.note: Mirrored over-the-shoulder hides the claw creature under the menu and puts the health panel over Tidus.

F46.note: Mirror of the corridor diagonal with the party on the right: clean, balanced and easy to read.

S01.note: Reads like a real console JRPG: every story beat gets its own shot, and the worm's-eye colossus and low victory angle are trailer material; only the opening over-the-shoulder command frame is cramped.

S02.note: The bands keep the HUD tidy, but moving the camera for every menu page (high for magic, close for items) would get busy fast.

S03.note: The push-in on Paine looks great, but the pink flower reticle over a blurred dragon is confusing and the camera moves on every menu hop.

S04.note: The orbit to the far side is pretty, but the near-black frame while the column covers the screen reads like a glitch, and orbiting every turn would tire me.

S05.note: Hard cuts are crisper than glides and the over-the-shoulder attack shot with the target bracket is strong, but cutting on every menu page is a lot.

S06.note: Paine's cut-in is the most stylish single frame in the strips and going behind each active girl tells me whose turn it is, but the backs hide the dragon and a cut-in every turn could wear thin.

S07.note: The low, close three-quarter shots of Tidus are gorgeous, but blurring the target I am attacking is backwards and a crane or dolly on every menu page would tire me.

S08.note: The close-behind-Paine item shot is mostly white hair, and the flower reticle again reads as a mystery overlay.

S09.note: Kimahri's cut-in with his name in huge type is pure trailer candy and the craned enemy attack reads well; the behind-the-shoulder command frame is cramped.

S10.note: Whip-pan smears on every menu choice look like dropped frames and would be exhausting every turn.

S11.note: Nothing moves, so it is always clear and never tiring, but it is static and the flower reticle is the only flourish.

S12.note: Rock-steady and clean with a simple target bracket; reads instantly but gives a trailer nothing to cut to.

S13.note: The red-lit Mega Flare wind-up and the leaping victory shot are showstoppers; the opening over-the-shoulder with the giant flower reticle is the one cluttered beat.

S14.note: Half the frames are motion-blur smears; as the per-menu behaviour it would feel nauseating.

top5.reason: On a phone it looks like a finished premium release: the villain looms over the heroes' backs like a poster, and the buttons and health cards are big and obvious.
The most cinematic desktop frame: snow, a villain towering beyond the heroes' shoulders, and every number tucked into clean letterbox bands so the painting stays whole.
The heroine turns toward me with the dragon on the right, so I get faces, the threat and a tidy HUD in one glance.
The dragon rears over the three girls' backs with room to breathe and the HUD kept to the corners: dramatic and still clear.
Bright soft-focus blue with the whole party visible in a clean diagonal toward the villain: the polished classic-JRPG look (F07 and F46 are close behind).

bottom3.reason: Portrait tokens on a blue map: no world, no characters, it looks like a debug view rather than a game.
The villain crowds the menu in the foreground while the heroes are specks far away with a name tag on Kimahri; I cannot tell which side is mine.
A giant Tidus face with the menu across his chest and a pixelated seam into the villain reads as a broken collage (F25 has the same problem).

topSequences.reason: The camera changes on story beats rather than menu pages (hit, reverse for the enemy turn, worm's-eye for the big attack, low hero angle for victory) and every frame is trailer material.
The dragon-fight counterpart: the red-lit Mega Flare wind-up and the leaping victory shot are showstoppers; only the flower-reticle opener is cluttered.
Kimahri's cut-in with his name in huge type is pure style, and going behind the active character tells me whose turn it is.

wholeGame: If the whole game looked like F28 and F38 I would wishlist it on sight: both push every number into clean letterbox bands so the painting stays whole, F28 gives the looming-villain-beyond-the-heroes'-shoulders drama and F38 turns the heroine toward me with the dragon waiting on the right, so I see faces and the threat in one glance. Put S01's camera language (and S13's for the dragon fight) on top of that, a calm command view, then a cut for the hit, a reverse for the enemy turn, a worm's-eye for the big attack and a low hero angle for victory, and it plays like a real console JRPG rather than a menu over a picture; on a phone, F23 is the translation to keep. F29 and F24 are the most striking stills in the set, but they are key art rather than battle screens (no HUD, heroes with their backs to the boss), and nothing should move the camera on every menu page the way the whip pans in S10 and S14 or the blackout orbit in S04 do.
